title: From Growth to Visibility: Bureaucratic Incentives After China's Cadre Evaluation Reforms
text:
President Xi Jinping has spent more than a decade trying to reform the incentive system of China's bureaucracy, especially the incentives for local governments. Xi launched sweeping reforms of the cadre evaluation system—reducing the emphasis on GDP growth, expanding performance assessments to include social welfare and environmental protection metrics, and strengthening inspections of policy implementation. These reforms were intended to shift bureaucratic incentives away from short-term political performance and toward more balanced governance.Yet a different pattern has emerged. Local governments, especially at the level of township and county, have increasingly devoted resources to highly visible "spotlight projects" (亮点工程) designed to attract the attention of higher-level leaders in municipalities and provinces. This outcome is not a failure of implementation but an unintended consequence of Xi's reforms. By broadening evaluation criteria while tightening fiscal and administrative constraints, the reforms changed how local officials compete for promotion. Instead of maximizing GDP growth, officials increasingly compete by producing politically visible success stories that signal competence and alignment with central priorities. Because these projects also enhance the political standing of provincial and municipal leaders, they are reinforced by complementary incentives at multiple levels of the bureaucracy. The result is not the disappearance of performative governance, but its transformation.

Reforming the Cadre Evaluation System

For decades, building a Weberian rational-legal, meritocratic bureaucracy has been central to the resilience of the Chinese political system. The foundation for this system lay in the cadre management system, particularly its performance-based promotion mechanism. In the pre-Xi era, local cadres in China were tasked with numerous responsibilities and targets, some of which might be mutually contradictory. These targets were categorized into two types: “hard targets,” which are binding and involve measurable outcomes, and “soft targets,” which are nonbinding and lack measurable criteria. Local leaders prioritized achieving hard targets over soft ones because the former carried greater weight in performance evaluations, leading to the problem of selective policy implementation. For example, local government officials were tasked with generating industrial growth while protecting the local environment. The result was often local governments ignoring environmental regulations to pursue industrial growth. Among these targets, GDP growth had historically been one of the most significant hard targets. It even became a veto target, meaning that failure to meet the GDP growth target could override and nullify all other accomplishments. Other notable veto targets included maintaining social stability and, before the abolition of the one-child policy, implementing birth control policies. This intense focus on GDP growth spurred tournament-style competition among local governments, with officials adopting growth-maximization strategies to enhance their own prospects for promotion. Paradoxically, this same GDP-driven system—even though it distorts policy priorities—has also been identified by scholars as a key driver of China’s rapid economic growth during the Reform Era.Although the outcome-based nature of the cadre evaluation system in the pre-Xi era drove remarkable economic growth, it simultaneously generated several structural and governance problems. Most importantly, since GDP growth is the most vital indicator of the cadre evaluation, local cadres blindly pursued GDP growth at all costs, which led to problems such as pollution, overcapacity, and surging local debt. In response, Xi sought to reform the cadre evaluation system by declaring that GDP could not be the primary criterion of promotion, and that assessments using the new evaluation system must also reflect social progress, welfare, environment, and other indicators. In December 2013, the Central Organization Department released a notice on reforming the cadre evaluation system. The document downplayed the role of economic growth, stating that GDP would no longer be the primary basis for evaluation results and/or promotion. “Sustainable economic development and livelihood improvement, social harmony and progress, cultural development, ecological civilization construction, and Party building” would also become important evaluation criteria. To implement the changes, Xi centralized the cadre evaluation reform by shifting the power of evaluating policy implementation to the vertical line of higher-level governments. As a result, upper-level government introduced post-implementation inspections as an instrument to evaluate the effectiveness and compliance of policy implementation processes. For example, the upper-level social security bureau (人社局) inspects lower-level social security offices in delivering employment assistance and other social services, which were previously largely overlooked by local government. During these inspections, teams from higher-level governments review files documenting each step of the enforcement process. Typically, these files include documents, meeting records, and even photographs taken throughout the policy implementation process. These file inspections (查台账) play a crucial role in enforcing Xi’s vision of a balanced cadre evaluation system. Overall, it allows for the evaluation of previously unmeasurable targets, making the policy evaluation system more balanced in theory. As a result, local cadres must actively implement these policies rather than disregard them.Although the evaluation reforms broadened the range of policy areas considered in cadre evaluations, they did not eliminate the scarcity of local government resources. Instead, local officials now faced a growing number of performance targets while operating under increasingly constrained fiscal and administrative capacity. As a result, they could no longer concentrate resources on a single objective such as GDP growth, nor could they realistically excel across every evaluation category. Faced with these trade-offs, local governments became increasingly selective in allocating resources and administrative attention. Rather than pursuing comprehensive improvements across all policy areas, officials concentrated substantive resources on a small number of highly visible projects while satisfying inspection requirements in other areas primarily through documentation and procedural compliance. Well-publicized projects in strategically important sectors could simultaneously demonstrate policy implementation, innovation, and responsiveness to central priorities, allowing officials to signal competence more efficiently than through broad-based improvements in governance. It is under these institutional conditions that spotlight projects emerged as an increasingly attractive strategy for career advancement.A “spotlight project” (亮点工程) functions as a form of political advertisement for the local government. Like the “vanity projects” of the 2000s, the primary goals of a spotlight project are to attract the attention of higher-level leaders and signal local competence. However, the top leadership has come to view the large-scale infrastructure projects of the past as costly “white elephants,” and they now carry significant political risks and may even trigger disciplinary action (as in the case of former Liuzhou Party Secretary Zheng Junkang). Instead, spotlight projects typically take the form of local economic development initiatives that align closely with national policy priorities or the interests of superior officials, and are deliberately designed to generate public visibility. As the “GDP tournament” no longer determines cadre promotion, local officials have increasingly relied on spotlight projects to demonstrate their achievements. Rather than competing primarily through economic growth, local leaders seek to transmit “success stories” upward and build a reputation for competence. In practice, however, many of these spotlight projects are largely performative rather than genuinely transformative. Given their limited terms in office, local officials have strong incentives to produce visible achievements quickly, whereas the outcomes of substantive policy implementation unfold gradually and are often realized only after the Party secretary's tenure has ended. Moreover, creating genuinely successful projects typically requires substantial upfront investment. For example, the Hefei municipal government invested approximately RMB 7 billion in NIO in 2020 to rescue the electric vehicle manufacturer from bankruptcy—a strategy that ultimately proved successful but required enormous fiscal commitment. Although spotlight projects at the township and county levels are much smaller in scale, they likewise demand significant public investment, which has become increasingly difficult under mounting fiscal constraints. Consequently, rather than investing in the long-term success of these projects, local officials often devote greater effort to making them simply appear successful. As one official explained, local leaders frequently enlist journalists to secure favorable coverage in national or provincial newspapers, and commission scholars to write policy memoranda highlighting local achievements for circulation among higher-level officials. The objective is to attract the attention of senior leaders and leave a favorable impression. In some cases, interviewees even reported that lower-level officials attempted to influence access channels—for example, by bribing the personal staff of higher-level Party secretaries—to ensure that these favorable materials reached the leaders' desks.These spotlight projects are equally valuable for higher-level leaders, particularly provincial and municipal officials. Most spotlight projects are designed around policy priorities emphasized by the central leadership. In recent years, they have been concentrated in areas such as technological innovation, tourism, and rural economic development, corresponding closely to Xi Jinping's priorities of technological self-reliance, greater domestic consumption, and rural revitalization. By fostering successful spotlight projects within their jurisdictions, provincial and municipal leaders can demonstrate their own effectiveness in implementing central directives, and thus strengthen their political credentials. Speaking in 2026, an official from Baise, Guangxi explained the importance of supporting local projects: “When Vice Premier Liu Guozhong visited us in 2024, we needed spotlight projects to show him our success.” This creates a shared incentive between higher- and lower-level officials. Grassroots leaders use spotlight projects to gain visibility and signal competence, while provincial and municipal leaders benefit from these projects because they showcase the successful implementation of central priorities within their jurisdictions. As several cadres explained in interviews, higher-up leaders are likely to promote grassroots officials who “follow their lead (紧跟领导)” and “solve problems for them (为领导分忧),” and producing local success stories in prioritized policy areas certainly fits the criteria. Spotlight projects persist not because local officials are deceiving their superiors, but because they satisfy the political incentive structures of both higher- and lower-level officials.The following case studies illustrate how this dynamic operates in practice.

Case Study I: Innovation in Shanghai

In 2022, Chen Jining became the Party secretary of Shanghai. Chen is widely regarded as part of Xi Jinping’s cohort of “technocratic” officials—leaders with strong backgrounds in science and technology. Prior to his political career, Chen was a leading environmental scientist; he earned his doctorate from Imperial College London and later served as a professor and president at Tsinghua University. It is widely understood that Xi has promoted such technocratic officials to strengthen China’s capacity for domestic technological innovation.Chen has shown a particular interest in technological innovation, especially its application to economic growth, public administration, and urban governance. One of his flagship initiatives is the development of a “quantum city,” a framework that seeks to integrate big data, quantum computing, and artificial intelligence into urban planning and governance. In a speech in February 2026, Chen emphasized that Shanghai must “strengthen technological empowerment to enhance governance capacity,” highlighting the quantum city initiative and big data-driven government platforms as key instruments. He also attended a Quantum City Annual Conference, signaling his personal commitment to this agenda.Local officials in Shanghai have sought to align themselves with Chen’s agenda by launching “spotlight projects” under the banner of the quantum city. Many of these projects focus on integrating technologies into government platforms. For example, Jinshan District established Shanghai’s first “digital public service center,” intended to serve as a major data exchange platform for government agencies and private firms alike. Jinshan has also positioned itself as a frontrunner in promoting “smart government” through the adoption of Office Automation (OA) systems. The Shanghai municipal government approved of Jinshan’s OA system so much that the company that built it later won the contract to build an OA system for the Shanghai municipal government, according to a Shanghai official. However, according to multiple officials, the implementation has been deeply flawed. Interviewees described the OA system as “rudimentary” and “a waste of money.” More broadly, some cadres characterized the “quantum city” initiative as largely performative—“a show without substance”—arguing that the primary motivation behind local efforts was simply to signal alignment with Chen’s priorities. Nevertheless, such signaling appears to have yielded political returns. The Party secretary of Jinshan, Liu Jian, was recently promoted to head Shanghai’s Development and Reform Commission, making him one of the city’s most influential economic policymakers. While there might be many reasons for the appointment, many Shanghai officials claimed that Liu’s ability to appeal to Chen’s interests in technological governance certainly played a major role in his rise. 

Case Study II: Rural Economic Development in Guangxi

Another illustrative example of a “spotlight project” involves rural economic development in Guangxi. Rural revitalization is one of Xi Jinping’s signature policy initiatives. Accordingly, in a predominantly rural region such as Guangxi, development has become a top priority. Guangxi is often referred to as “China’s fruit basket” due to its abundant fruit production, which has long served as a pillar of the local economy. In recent years, the emphasis on poverty alleviation and rural revitalization has led local governments to prioritize the development of agricultural industries, as these sectors are expected to generate higher-value employment opportunities beyond traditional farming. Following central policy directives, a county near Nanning sought to move beyond orange harvesting and wholesaling—activities that local farmers increasingly viewed as “profitless” —toward the development of a branded local orange juice product. The local government promoted this product as a regional “name card,” with the ambition of expanding its market presence nationwide. According to one local cadre, county leaders—including the Party secretary—view the orange-processing industry as a key component of the local economy. The county governor even brought the orange juice product to the 2025 Guangxi provincial “Two Sessions” to showcase this initiative as a model of local achievement.However, the resulting juice was terrible and poorly suited for broader commercial expansion. Instead of producing high-quality not-from-concentrate juice using fresh local oranges—a segment of China’s beverage market that has been gaining popularity—the company opted to blend orange juice concentrate with citrus additives, resulting in a sour and bitter taste. Even local farmers described the product in interviews as “distasteful” and “shameful for our oranges.” To market this product, the local government relied on highly visible promotional campaigns. In 2024, the county organized a series of juice-tasting events in Harbin, leveraging the surge in winter tourism in the region, and distributed over 110,000 bottles of juice. Local officials framed these events as a breakthrough in the effort to enter the national market, and the campaign received favorable coverage from Xinhua News Agency.Subsequently, the product continued to receive positive media attention and drew interest from the Guangxi provincial government. It was even featured at the China-ASEAN Expo and promoted as a model case of rural industrial development outside of Guangxi. Despite this extensive publicity, however, the product has made little tangible progress in expanding its market share. The reported “success” in official narratives is not supported by observable market performance. Ironically, while local leaders aspire to national expansion, the juice is not even widely available in supermarkets in Nanning, the provincial capital.While it is still too early to assess the impact of this juice initiative on the careers of local leaders, the case illustrates a broader pattern associated with “spotlight projects.” As the Shanghai example suggests, such projects are perceived by officials as an important pathway to promotion. This has produced a shared understanding among cadres that, while launching a successful spotlight project may not be sufficient for advancement, it has become a necessary condition for entering the consideration set of higher-level leaders. As a result, local officials are incentivized to initiate spotlight projects simply to keep pace with their peers and avoid falling behind politically.

Will Xi’s new campaign solve the problem?

In 2026, Xi Jinping has launched a campaign to study “correct view on political achievement” (正确政绩观) as a solution to the cadre incentive problem. According to Xi, the “view on political achievement” reflects cadres’ “world view, outlook on life, and values.” A correct view on political achievement is fundamentally people-centered: Officials must pursue achievements for the benefit of the people and not for selfish interests. In addition, it requires pursuing substantive, sustainable, and verifiable achievements that promote high-quality development, meet the needs of the people, and serve the broader national interests. Overall, a correct view of political achievement is a reality-based, ethically grounded standard of governance, where officials are expected to work for the people, produce genuine and sustainable outcomes, and achieve those outcomes through integrity, competence, and hard work.Xi has argued that the absence of a “correct view on political achievement” is a source of persistent problems within the Chinese bureaucracy, including resource waste, corruption, and formalism. In a 2013 speech, Xi identified “selfishness” as the root cause of these cadre-related problems. At the National Conference on Organizational Work in July 2018, Xi further observed: “Some cadres lack the energy and spirit to perform their duties with creativity; they avoid taking responsibility and fail to take action. They are afraid of making mistakes in decision-making, dare not make decisions, and tend to shirk responsibilities and procrastinate in their work.” In a January 2026 group study session for provincial-level cadres, Xi elaborated that a “wrong view on political achievement” originates from the interests of individuals or small groups. It is characterized by impatience, a fixation on quick results, falsification and deception, and reckless decision-making. He said that such a mindset encourages the pursuit of “image projects” and “showcase achievements,” resulting in long-term burdens and hidden risks and ultimately provoking strong public dissatisfaction.In general, Xi attributes the current problems in the Chinese bureaucracy to factors at the individual level. Issues such as cadre inaction, formalism, and corruption are understood to be the result of officials lacking a “correct view on political achievement.” Accordingly, his proposed solution is to instill this “correct view” in all officials, on the assumption that such political indoctrination will lead to improved bureaucratic behavior. However, while it is true that many local officials do not align with Xi’s “correct view,” blaming individual cadres does not solve the structural issues discussed above. The likelier outcome is that the campaign—which has now been underway for years—provokes negative reactions from local cadres, who then resort to formalism, the exact behavior the campaign aims to eliminate, to deal with the campaign’s onerous demands. One cadre joked about the anti-formalism campaign that “once we receive the central document on anti-formalism, we have a big study session on this topic. During the meeting, we make sure to leave traces such as taking pictures. Afterward, we must write up a report on the study session, so we can have a complete file for the upcoming anti-formalism inspection.” “Indeed,” the cadre concluded, “we are fighting formalism with formalism.”
